Q: apache beam rows to tfrecord in order to GenerateStatistics A:

What you're bringing up is the distinction between components in tfx and the underlying libraries. Since the components interact via on-disk artifacts, they require tfrecords (e.g. you can attach a StatisticsGen component and accomplish what you're looking to do). But let's say you wanted to not use components, and use the libraries directly. TFX BSL provides the ability to go from something like a NamedTuple object straight to a pyarrow RecordBatch, which would help you get things done at the "library" level. The way I think of it is a beam transform (which these libraries provide) can be used in a TFX Executor to move from library oriented thinking to component oriented thinking. The beam paradigm (PCollections, PTransforms) is the most flexible layer, but you may just want to use the components to abstract/avoid that complexity. For example, you may want to do statistics by windows of time. In this case, you'd want to use the transforms provided by TFDV and produce the pyarrow RecordBatches to accomplish this. Hope this helps.

Q: Is making in-place operations return the object a bad idea? A:

If you mean operations like +=, then absolutely, as the variable gets bound to the return value of the operation. This allows you to make out-of-place in-place operations.

If you mean methods like list.sort (as you gave in the question), then to be consistent, you should return None or something else important.

Q: How can I get Unicode output from robocopy in a PowerShell script? A:

As of the rococopy.exe version that comes with Windows 11 25H2, the /unicode option appears to be broken: only a (small) part of the output is actually UTF-16LE ("Unicode") encoded, resulting in garbled output if the entire output is decoded as UTF-16LE, which is what you experienced.[1]

As a workaround, you can use the /unilog:<target-file> option to directly save the output to a (properly) UTF-16LE-encoded file, preceded by the appropriate BOM.

Therefore (note the /unilog: option):

$sourcedir = $env:PUBLIC
$destdir = $env:TEMP
$logpath = $env:USERPROFILE + "\test-robo-uni.txt"
$null = 
  robocopy.exe $sourcedir $destdir /unilog:$logpath /E /L /S /E /DCOPY:DA /COPY:DAT /NP /R:1 /W:1

Note:

  • Since robocopy itself writes its output to the target file with "Unicode" encoding, independently of the current console settings, there is no need to modify [Console]::OutputEncoding.

  • $null = suppresses the message indicating successful creation of the target log file that robocopy prints to stdout.

  • As an aside: Unlike in POSIX-compatible shells such as Bash, in PowerShell there is no need to "..."-enclose variable references: PowerShell properly passes even variable values that contain spaces (or other metacharacters) correctly as-is; e.g., as shown above, use $sourcedir, not "$sourcedir".

[1] Your approach of (temporarily) setting [Console]::OutputEncoding to [System.Text.Encoding]::Unicode (i.e. UTF-16LE) - so as to make PowerShell interpret robocopy's output as UTF-16LE before storing it as a .NET string in $output (the same approach as in the answer to the linked Select-String question) - would have been correct if robocopy /unicode worked as advertised (produced proper UTF-16LE output), but the problem is that it doesn't.
For a systematic overview of how PowerShell interacts with external programs with respect to character encoding, see this answer.
